sn29.1:1.1: Thus begins a series of four Saṁyuttas on various nonhuman entities.
sn29.1:1.2: The “dragon” (_nāga_) is a powerful ([pli-tv-bu-vb-pc51:1.4]()) serpentine ([sn1.37:7.4](), [cp20:1.2]()) entity with fiery breath ([sn3.1:8.2]()), bearing magical gems ([pli-tv-bu-vb-ss6:1.3.2](), [ja253]()). They dwell underground ([mn23:2.39]()), or in the ocean ([ud5.5:17.1]()), or in the mountains ([sn46.1:1.2]()), guarding treasure ([ja506]()) that they may have stolen ([kp8:4.3]()). They may be man-eaters ([sn6.4:9.2]()) or protectors ([ud2.1:2.2]()), and occasionally had to be engaged in magical combat ([pli-tv-kd1:15.2.3]()), [pli-tv-bu-vb-pc51:1.4]()). They are color-changers ([sn3.1:8.1](), [cp13:3.1]()) and shape-shifters who, though they revert when they sleep, can temporarily take human form ([pli-tv-kd1:63.1.1]()), even for the purpose of intimate relations ([pli-tv-bu-vb-pj1:10.14.1]()). The line between the supernatural entity and organic snakes is as fluid as a serpent’s form; dragons act as the leaders and protectors of all snakes ([pli-tv-kd6:23.13.5]()), while poorly behaved dragons may be banished to a snake’s existence ([ja304]()). Powerful and feared though they are, they are still no match for the cruelest of predators, man ([ja524]()). For a history of the word, see [sn46.1:1.2]().
sn29.1:1.4: These four are defined at [mn12:32.1](); see note there for Vedic and Jain sources. | The Dhammic import of this idea is that even such powerful entities are born, and hence are subject to old age and death.
